bp: A large video platform has to decide, every day, which videos may create a safety problem before many viewers are exposed to them. The paper focuses on adult-content issue detection inside recommendation, where the practical job is not only to understand a video, but to place risky videos high enough in an internal inspection or filtering order that action can happen in time. Existing systems often ask a large multimodal language model to read sampled frames and captions. That can be accurate, but the abstract says it is slow to update, expensive to serve, and narrow in what it sees. A video's risk is not only inside its pixels or words. It may also appear in user reactions after publication, in patterns attached to the video, and in signals about the author. This paper serves the platform need to keep a recommendation system responsive: safety evidence changes daily, so the scoring system must also change daily.
wh: The hard part is that content safety is both a perception problem and an operations problem. A sampled frame or caption can reveal some adult content, but a platform must score all videos, not just a small hand-picked set, and it must do so often enough that new risky items do not wait for a monthly or quarterly refresh. The obvious high-accuracy tool, a large multimodal language model, brings three pressures named in the abstract: poor timeliness, limited feature richness, and high serving cost. Poor timeliness matters because recommendations happen continuously, while content and user reactions change after upload. Limited feature richness matters because intrinsic video features miss post-hoc user feedback and aggregated video and author-side signals. High serving cost matters because the platform needs daily scoring at broad scale. The tension is therefore precision versus reach: a heavy judge may read one case well, but the platform needs a lighter judge that can revisit the whole pile.
naive: A smart beginner would run the strongest available multimodal model on each video, using sampled frames and captions, then flag videos whose adult-content score crosses a threshold. That is natural because the suspected issue seems to live inside the video itself. The approach breaks when the platform context changes faster than the model is refreshed. If the score is updated only monthly or quarterly, yesterday's user feedback and author behavior cannot affect today's recommendation safety. It also treats external evidence as secondary even though viewers' reactions and author-level patterns may reveal risk that a few frames or captions miss. Finally, doing this for all videos every day can be too costly, so the model may be accurate in principle but too heavy for the serving job.
ap: The paper's central move is to turn content issue detection into a daily ranking problem. Instead of relying mainly on a large model's direct reading of video samples, it builds a smaller scoring model that can be refreshed at day level and can combine several kinds of evidence. The Cross-Order Representation Fusion architecture, as described by the abstract, is the part that fuses signals that come from different orders or levels: user behavior after the video is shown, video-side information, author-side information, and scores produced by the larger multimodal model. The big model is not thrown away; its score becomes one input among others. The smaller model then assigns risk scores efficiently enough to cover all videos each day. The core idea is triage by fused evidence: use the expensive reader as a signal, but let fresh platform behavior and author context help decide which videos are most risky now.
mech: The mechanism begins with the video population that the platform may recommend. For each video, the system gathers several input streams named in the abstract. One stream is user behavior: signals produced after users interact with or respond to the video. Another is video-side information, which can include aggregated properties about the video beyond a few sampled frames or captions. A third is author-side information, which summarizes evidence attached to the account or creator. A fourth is the score from a multimodal large language model, a large system that examines visual and textual video content and estimates issue risk. CORF then has to make these unlike signals comparable enough for one decision. In plain terms, it builds internal descriptions for the different evidence sources, combines them through its fusion architecture, and produces a single ranking score for content issue detection. The model is updated daily, so newly accumulated behavior and aggregated signals can enter the next scoring pass. Once scores are produced, all videos can be ordered by estimated adult-content issue risk. The evaluation then checks whether, at the same precision level, the system finds more of the problematic videos than the MLLM-based baseline. Online A/B tests check the deployed consequence: whether users are exposed to fewer such content issues.
math: The main mathematical idea is ranking under limited attention. Ranking means turning many signs about each video into a score so the platform can sort a huge pile and focus action where risk is highest. The score is not a moral truth about the video; it is a practical ordering device. A second idea is feature fusion, which means combining measurements that describe different parts of the same case. Here the parts are video evidence, author evidence, user behavior, and an MLLM-generated score. Fusion is needed because no single source sees the whole problem: frames and captions see content, behavior sees post-publication reaction, and author-side signals see repeated context. A third idea is precision-recall tradeoff. Precision asks, among videos the system marks as risky, how many really are issues; recall asks, among true issues, how many the system catches. The paper reports higher recall at the same precision, which means it catches more adult-content cases without increasing the accepted false-alarm rate. There is also an efficiency tradeoff: a smaller model gives up some direct reading power of a large model, but gains daily coverage over all videos. The math fits because recommendation safety is a repeated sorting problem with fresh, noisy, multi-source evidence.
dots: This paper sits at the intersection of recommendation, ranking, multimodal content understanding, and responsible platform operation. It connects to the conference's broader ranking idea because the platform has too many videos for equal inspection and must decide which items deserve safety attention first. It also connects to multimodal vision-language work, but with an important twist: the large visual-language model is treated as one evidence source rather than the whole detector. That makes the paper closer to recommender-system papers that combine behavior, item, and creator signals than to papers that only classify media content. It also touches misinformation, trust, and safety themes, where the central problem is not simply predicting a label but reducing harmful exposure in a live web system. Compared with retrieval or recommendation papers that rank for usefulness or engagement, this one ranks for issue risk. The same mathematical shape appears, but the goal changes from pleasing the user to protecting the viewing environment.
ww: The approach should improve over the naive large-model-only strategy because it changes both the evidence and the refresh rhythm. More evidence helps when adult-content risk is not fully visible in a sampled view of the video. User behavior can reveal how real viewers respond after publication; video-side aggregates can capture patterns not present in a single caption; author-side information can carry repeated context across a creator's uploads; and the MLLM score still contributes the direct visual-textual reading. Daily updating helps because the ranking boundary is time-sensitive. If a video begins to receive suspicious feedback today, a monthly refresh leaves that signal unused for too long. A smaller model also helps operationally: if it can score all videos daily, the system can apply a consistent safety ordering across the whole recommendation pool rather than using an expensive detector on a narrower slice. The abstract's reported result, higher recall at the same precision, is exactly the expected benefit of richer evidence: more true issue cases rise above the action threshold without loosening the false-positive standard.
po: The payoff is a more practical safety layer for recommendations. The paper claims the model is significantly smaller than MLLM-based approaches, can score all videos daily, and integrates fresh behavior, video, author, and large-model score signals. In adult-content experiments, it finds more problematic videos at the same precision level, so the platform does not have to trade extra recall for a lower-quality flagged set. The online A/B tests matter because they move beyond offline scoring and report the user-facing effect: reduced exposure to adult-content issues. Grounded in the abstract, the contribution is not only better detection accuracy, but a cheaper, fresher ranking system for safer recommendations.
limits: The abstract supports the high-level mechanism but leaves several assumptions unproven. The method depends on user behavior, video-side aggregates, author-side information, and MLLM scores being available, timely, and not too biased by previous recommendation exposure. If risky videos are rarely shown, behavior feedback may be sparse; if author signals are overused, new or atypical creators could be judged unfairly. The evidence is reported for the Adult-Content category, so the abstract does not prove the same gains for other issue types. It also does not describe CORF's exact internal fusion steps, label quality, moderation policy boundary, false-positive impact on creators, or how adversaries might adapt once they learn which signals affect the daily ranking.
